claims.overstatement: 'About 20–28% lower in individual PET studies' is narrower than the studies this review reports. Johanson et al. (2006) found DAT (and VMAT2) 10–16% lower, and McCann et al. (2008) 13–23% lower (p. 596). Suggest 'about 10–28%'. The population phrase 'scanned after days to months of abstinence' also understates some samples: McCann et al. (1998) users averaged 32 ± 22 months abstinent (p. 592), and the McCann et al. (2008) imaging subset 77 ± 102 months (Table 2, p. 593).
claims.note: The rest of the claim is supported. Users lower on average; considerable overlap of individual values with controls (McCann 1998, p. 592; general statement p. 597); PET binding cannot distinguish toxicity from adaptation (p. 592). The pooled g and the specific percentages in the magnitude line do not come from this source. Hart et al. give Sekine et al. (2001) as about 20% lower (p. 592) and no percentages for McCann 1998.

anchors.locator: PET studies investigating DAT and DA receptor availability, 1st paragraph (right column)
anchors.extracted: McCann et al. (1998): 6 users abstinent on average 32 ± 22 months vs 10 controls; binding lower in caudate and putamen, but with considerable overlap (some users at or above some controls); all users used other illicit drugs.
Sekine et al. (2001): 11 users without other illicit drug histories vs 9 controls; striatal DAT about 20% lower.

Unclear whether a ~20% DAT difference lies within normal human variability or relates to cognition. Johanson et al. (2006): 16 users vs 18 controls, DAT and VMAT2 binding 10–16% lower. McCann et al. (2008): DAT 13–23% lower.

anchors.extracted: PET alone cannot establish dopaminergic neuronal toxicity because altered tracer binding may reflect adaptation rather than toxicity.

anchors.extracted: Several groups found lower striatal DAT and D2 levels in long-term users, with considerable overlap between users and controls.

claims.note: The claim already contains this source's contrary point ('another PET study found no relation between abstinence duration and transporter levels', i.e. McCann et al., 2008, as reported here). Hart et al. also report that in Johanson et al. (2006) neither imaging nor cognitive data correlated with abstinence duration. That is a second null study the claim could mention (and Volkow 2001a itself found r<0.11 with days since last use). The McCann 2008 imaging subset was small (7 users, 16 controls; Table 2, p. 593).

anchors.locator: Right column, paragraph beginning 'In general, studies using PET imaging…'
anchors.extracted: Some reports suggest extended abstinence increases DAT (Volkow et al., 2001d in this review's lettering, i.e. the recovery paper), others did not observe this (McCann et al., 2008); abstinence duration appears to have little effect on cognitive performance.

anchors.locator: Left column, 2nd paragraph (Johanson) and last paragraph (McCann 2008)
anchors.extracted: Johanson et al. (2006): neither imaging nor cognitive data correlated with abstinence duration. McCann et al. (2008): no relationship between abstinence duration and imaging or cognitive results.
Imaging subset: 7 users (abstinence mean 77.43 ± 102.21 months, range 8–300) vs 16 controls; DAT lower in bilateral caudate and left putamen.

claims.note: Supports the 'another research group found no difference in global metabolism' clause (London et al., 2004). The comparison is not like-for-like: London et al.'s users were abstinent 4–7 days, whereas Volkow 2001c's were 2 weeks to 35 months. Hart's Table 2 describes the Volkow metabolism paper's thalamic and striatal decreases without saying they were normalized (relative) values (p. 595).

anchors.locator: Right column, paragraph beginning 'In general, studies using PET imaging…'
anchors.extracted: Volkow et al. (2001a in this review's lettering, i.e. the metabolism paper) found higher absolute regional glucose metabolism in users; London et al. (2004) found no difference; many metabolic differences not replicated by independent groups.

14 users (diagnosis not reported) abstinent 4–7 days vs 13 controls; no difference in global glucose metabolism; lower relative metabolism in infragenual anterior cingulate, higher in ventral striatum; controls more educated.
15 users vs 21 controls; cognitive results not reported; education not reported; lower thalamic, caudate and putamen and higher parietal metabolism.

claims.note: Supports 'cannot distinguish loss from down-regulation' and the mixed recovery evidence. This source does not address the Parkinson's-disease pattern.

anchors.extracted: Dopaminergic neuronal toxicity cannot be determined from PET alone; binding changes may reflect adaptation rather than toxicity.
Whether a ~20% DAT difference lies within normal human variability, or relates to function, is unknown when cognition is not assessed.

anchors.locator: Right column, 'In general, studies using PET imaging…'
anchors.extracted: DAT increases with extended abstinence reported by one group but not observed by another; considerable overlap between users and controls.

claims.note: Table 1 lists 16 controlled laboratory dosing studies (pp. 590–591), described as double-blind within-participant designs (p. 589); the review concludes that disruptive effects were not observed and larger repeated doses remain untested (pp. 592, 604). Its account of the intranasal study fits the claim: all active doses improved reaction time, and only 12 and 25 mg improved visuospatial perception (DSST). Three caveats. (1) The text says sustained attention improved at all doses (p. 592), while Table 1 lists vigilance improved and sustained attention unchanged for the same study (p. 590). (2) 'Single-dose' is not exact for all 16: Comer et al. (2001) is titled as a study of repeated oral administration (reference list, p. 606). (3) In Silber et al. (2006), d-methamphetamine was worse than placebo on visuospatial processing in a first session (Table 1, p. 591), although Table 1 scores it as no effect. Several studies are marked as small (N=6–24).

anchors.extracted: Intranasal 0, 12, 25, 50 mg/70 kg in people with methamphetamine use disorder: all active doses improved reaction time and (per text) sustained attention; only 12 and 25 mg improved visuospatial perception; no disruption in any domain; repeated or binge dosing at larger doses untested.

16 laboratory studies (oral, intranasal, intravenous; N=6–24, within-participant): improvements in some domains in most; no consistent effect in two oral studies (Comer 2001; Hart 2001); no study scored as worsening; caveats include low doses, oral route, small samples and no repeated dosing.

Acute methamphetamine improved some domains (visuospatial perception, sustained attention, response speed) even at larger intranasal and intravenous doses; disruptive effects not observed; larger repeated doses would be needed for a fuller picture.

claims.note: 7/27 (25.9%) vs 2/18 (11.1%) recomputed. Hart's wording ('on average… approximately 7 of the 27 … in at least one domain', p. 602) leaves it unclear whether 7 is a count of users impaired in at least one domain or an average across domains. The claim should take the figure from Kalechstein et al. (2003) directly. Hart's Table 4 describes Kalechstein's users as current users with a negative urine on the test day (p. 603), while the text calls them abstinent (p. 602). The 16th–55th percentile range and the 34% vs 16% figure do not come from this source. Hart's normative comparisons of group means (Simon 2002; McCann 2008) are his own and give no norms or values.

anchors.extracted: Long-term users differed from controls on a minority of measures, and cognitive functioning overwhelmingly fell within the normal range against normative data.

anchors.locator: Comprehensive neuropsychological testing, 3rd paragraph (Kalechstein et al., 2003)
anchors.extracted: 27 users vs 18 controls; about 7 of 27 users vs 2 of 18 controls scored at least 2 SD below published norms in at least one domain (users more than twice as likely); in working memory, 2 controls (11%) vs 1 user (4%); most participants of both groups within the normal range.

By the reviewers' comparison with published norms, group mean scores of users in McCann et al. (2008) and Simon et al. (2002) were within the normal range, including on tests with significant group differences; Chang et al. (2002) users within the normal range on all standard tasks.

anchors.locator: Right column, last paragraph before 'PET studies investigating brain metabolism'
anchors.extracted: Distinguishes impairment as a statistical group difference from impairment as clinically meaningful loss of function; argues studies report the first and discuss the second.

claims.note: The review supports every element and goes further than the claim: it calls the impairment link not supported by research evidence (p. 605). The claim's 'not established' is the more defensible wording.

anchors.extracted: Single-time-point imaging cannot show that methamphetamine caused the differences; pre-existing group differences cannot be ruled out; controls had more schooling (15.2 vs 12.8 years).

anchors.locator: PET section summary; Tables 2–4 caveat columns
anchors.extracted: In most studies users reported extensive other drug use and controls little; controls frequently had more education; abstinence duration appears to have little effect on cognitive performance.

key_findings.correction: Two caveats. Text and Table 1 disagree for Hart et al. (2008): the text says sustained attention improved, Table 1 says vigilance improved and sustained attention unchanged (pp. 590, 592). 'Single doses' does not fit Comer et al. (2001), titled as a repeated-administration study (p. 606).
Hart's wording is 'on average … approximately 7 of the 27', which makes the count ambiguous; Table 4 (p. 603) lists these users as current users with a negative urine on the test day.
The metabolism-paper row (p. 595) also describes the thalamic and striatal decreases without noting that they were normalized values.

reporting_issues.note: An interpretive point rather than an internal inconsistency.

The lettering is internally consistent with Hart's own reference list (2001a metabolism, 2001b DAT, 2001c D2 receptors, 2001d recovery; pp. 607–608). It differs only from this encyclopedia's reference keys, so 'differs from their citation elsewhere' should read 'differs from the encyclopedia's keys'. The Wang et al. (2004) row does omit the Symbol Digit correlation (Table 2, p. 595): confirmed.

risk_of_bias.note: AMSTAR 2 critically low as a systematic summary agreed.

interpretation_gap.note: I would rate it moderate rather than minor, for the reasons the card itself gives: the conclusions move from 'not established' to 'not supported by evidence' and 'concerns not warranted' (p. 605). The abstract's 'overwhelmingly within the normal range' rests on a few unreported normative comparisons of group means. For consistency, I rated Dean et al. (2013), the opposing review, moderate as well.

missed: PET DAT differences smaller than 20%: Johanson et al. (2006) 10–16% and McCann et al. (2008) 13–23% (p. 596). These bear on the encyclopedia's 'about 20–28% lower in individual PET studies'. Johanson is in the card; McCann 2008's range is not.

Mixed DAT recovery evidence: DAT increases reported by the Volkow group but not observed by McCann et al. (2008), and no correlation with abstinence duration in Johanson et al. (2006) (pp. 596–597). Relevant to cl_meth_dat_recovery, for which this source is anchored as contradicting; not a key finding on the card.
Non-replication of higher global glucose metabolism by London et al. (2004; users abstinent 4–7 days) (p. 597; Table 2, p. 594). Relevant to cl_meth_glucose_metabolism; not a key finding on the card.
PET binding alone cannot establish dopaminergic toxicity, as changes may reflect adaptation (p. 592). Relevant to cl_meth_dopamine_damage; not a key finding.
Reporting issue: for Hart et al. (2008) the text (p. 592) and Table 1 (p. 590) disagree on whether sustained attention or vigilance improved.

Table 1 includes Comer et al. (2001), titled as a repeated-administration study (p. 606), and notes worse-than-placebo visuospatial processing in a first session with d-methamphetamine in Silber et al. (2006) (p. 591). Both are relevant to describing the 16 studies as single-dose with no worsening.
